strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically valuable: replacing gradient/Hessian-based influence estimation with a closed-form, forward-only score is a genuine efficiency advance, and the complexity analysis (Tab. 3) and runtime benchmarks (Fig. 4, seconds vs. hours, scaling to 72B parameters) substantiate the efficiency claims convincingly.

The paper derives its score from an explicit (if idealized) learning-dynamics analysis (Theorems 1–2, Appendix 8.2), giving the method a principled basis rather than pure heuristic similarity, and the ablation on the α (prediction-error) term shows it is doing real work beyond embedding similarity.

Experiments cover both LLMs and VLMs, multiple model families and sizes (1.5B–72B), three task types, and two applications (influential-example identification and mislabeled-data detection), with reasonable baselines including the recent and strong HyperINF and an adapted embedding-based method.

The setup, prompts, dataset statistics, metrics, and baseline training details are documented in enough detail (Appendix 8.3–8.4) that the study appears largely reproducible, and license/data attribution is addressed.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation rests on a very strong idealization: the 'unconstrained features' assumption treats every per-token hidden state of every training and validation sample as a freely trainable parameter of the model. This decouples the analysis from actual SGD dynamics over network weights, so Theorem 1 does not establish that the score approximates true influence in real fine-tuning; the paper does not empirically validate the approximation quality against ground-truth influence (e.g., leave-one-out retraining), which is the standard sanity check in this literature.

The evaluation protocol is weak as a proxy for influence: 'influential data identification' uses class-membership pseudo-labels on small, highly templated synthetic datasets (900 training samples, 10 classes), and near-saturated AUC/Recall (1.000 everywhere) suggests the task may be solvable by trivial similarity and does not test fine-grained per-sample influence. No real-world, diverse downstream datasets (e.g., the harder or human-annotated settings used in prior work) are evaluated.

A fairness concern in the comparison: baselines (Hessian-free, DataInf, HyperINF) estimate influence for a fine-tuned model, whereas For-Value scores the pretrained model without any fine-tuning. The paper does not disentangle whether For-Value wins because of a better score or because the baselines suffer from checkpoint-selection instability that For-Value avoids by construction; the 'best-checkpoint' baseline selection partially mitigates but does not resolve this.

Assumption 2 (no training input equals the valuation input) is claimed 'mild' but is central to dropping Term (II); for text tasks, near-duplicate or identical-prefix inputs are common in practice, and the paper offers no empirical measurement of when this breaks.

Some reported comparisons are ambiguous (e.g., Tab. 2 subject generation: For-Value recall 0.897 vs. HyperINF 0.902 on Qwen-VL, yet the text claims a >7% recall gain 'for both models for the 11B model'); Emb baseline appears to have copy-paste-identical numbers across the two VLM models; no code release or statistical significance testing is mentioned.

The paper cites no prior forward-only/last-layer influence approximations it might be closest to (e.g., TracIn on the last layer, functional similarity / representation-based influence works), leaving the novelty positioning somewhat under-argued beyond gradient-based baselines.

strengths: The proposed method is genuinely simple and highly efficient: requiring only a single forward pass and restricting computation to the in-batch vocabulary makes it orders of magnitude faster than gradient/Hessian-based baselines, and the paper credibly demonstrates scalability up to 72B-parameter models that baselines cannot feasibly process.

The empirical evaluation is broad along several axes: multiple LLMs (1.5B–72B) and VLMs (3B, 11B), three LLM task types, two VLM task types, a mislabeled-data detection task, an ablation of the prediction-error term, runtime analysis, and qualitative examples.

The core intuition—that influence under a likelihood objective relates to hidden-representation alignment weighted by prediction-error similarity—is clearly stated, and the closed-form implementation (Eq. 2, Algorithm 1) is described at a level that supports reimplementation.

The paper connects to and clearly differentiates from relevant prior work (DataInf, HyperINF, TracIn, Shapley-in-run, GMValuator), addressing a real practical gap: data valuation when gradients and fine-tuned checkpoints are unavailable.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation rests on a very strong and nonstandard assumption: the proof treats per-sample hidden embeddings h_{x,y,<k} as trainable parameters of the model (the parameter vector θ in the appendix includes all embeddings), which is not how LLM/VLM fine-tuning actually works (weights, or LoRA adapters, are trained; hidden states are functions of inputs). The derived score therefore may not correspond to real training dynamics, and the paper provides no empirical validation that the score tracks actual likelihood changes d/dt ln π during fine-tuning.

The evaluation metric is a weak proxy for influence: AUC/Recall are computed against pseudo-labels based on class membership between training and validation samples, following DataInf. This does not measure whether identified samples actually change model predictions or likelihood on validation data—the quantity the method and theory target. No ground-truth influence experiment (e.g., retrain-or-finetune leave-one-out checks, or correlation of scores with actual likelihood gains) is reported.

The tasks appear trivially separable, undermining the strength of the reported (often perfect, 1.000 AUC) results. Notably, the appendix states that 'unique identifying chatbot names were prepended to the task prompt to assist the model in training,' which leaks class identity into the input; surface-level lexical similarity between prompts could plausibly yield perfect AUC regardless of genuine influence modeling. The mislabeled-detection task (50% label flip on a binary cat/dog task where baselines reach 1.0) is also far easier than realistic noise settings.

All datasets are small synthetic setups (900 training samples, 10 classes; 600 VLM pairs; 800 images). There is no evaluation on realistic-scale data valuation scenarios (e.g., instruction-tuning corpora, web-scale deduplication or filtering), limiting evidence for the practical claims of applicability to real LLM/VLM deployment.

The complexity accounting is incomplete: while the score computation itself is cheap, For-Value still requires a forward pass over the entire training set for each valuation sample (or batch of valuation samples), i.e., O(n) full inference passes, which is a substantial cost at realistic data scale and should be analyzed explicitly rather than folded away.

Several design choices are under-justified or unexplored: which layer's hidden state is used, sensitivity to the α formulation, behavior when inputs are near-duplicates (the paper's Assumption 2 explicitly excludes identical inputs, but near-duplicate/boilerplate-heavy corpora are precisely the practical regime where this matters), and no comparison against an additional validation-time baseline such as perplexity-based ranking.

Reproducibility support is thin: no code release is mentioned, no reproducibility statement, and several experimental details (e.g., how baselines are tuned across checkpoints, hyperparameters of For-Value, seeds) are only partially specified. Baselines are reported at the checkpoint with the highest test AUC, a selection procedure that is itself acknowledged as unstable.

Presentation issues: duplicated references (Bai et al. 2025a/b are the same Qwen2.5-VL report), typos (e.g., 'Most Influencial'), and citation formatting problems suggest the manuscript is not yet polished.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: a forward-only, closed-form data valuation score that eliminates gradients, Hessian computations, and fine-tuning, addressing a genuine scalability gap for billion-parameter LLMs and VLMs where existing influence methods are impractical.

The theoretical derivation (Theorems 1-2, Appendix 8.2) is presented in full and transparently states its assumptions (unconstrained features, distinct inputs), grounding the score in learning dynamics of the teacher-forcing objective.

Experiments follow the established DataInf evaluation protocol (AUC/Recall with class-based pseudo-labels), covering multiple models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen2.5 series up to 72B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision), multiple task types, and both influential-sample identification and mislabeled-data detection.

The efficiency evaluation is thorough for the proposed method: runtime benchmarks from 1.5B to 72B, complexity comparison table (Tab. 3), and a practical in-batch vocabulary restriction with a clear algorithm (Alg. 1). The ablation isolating the prediction-error term α from pure embedding similarity is informative and shows the added value over a naive similarity baseline.
Qualitative examples (Fig. 3) support the claim that rankings are semantically meaningful (matching task rules, subjects, styles).
weaknesses: The theory rests on a very strong and unrealistic assumption: treating hidden embeddings h_{x,y<k} as free trainable parameters independent of the network weights (Assumption 1). The proof effectively ignores gradients through the transformer layers (attention, MLPs), which are precisely where cross-sample influence flows during fine-tuning. The derivation therefore justifies the score only under a heavily simplified model, and the gap between this idealization and real learning dynamics is not quantified empirically (e.g., no validation of the score against ground-truth leave-one-out retraining or likelihood changes).

The evaluation tasks are small-scale and synthetic (900 training samples, 10 templated classes; cats-vs-dogs with 50% synthetic label flips). The influence metric is a class-matching pseudo-label proxy, and many results are saturated (AUC = 1.000 for several methods and models), limiting the evidence's ability to discriminate between methods or to demonstrate utility on realistic valuation scenarios such as large web-scale corpora.

The paper never validates the central claim of data valuation in its most consequential form: no experiment shows that selecting or removing data based on For-Value scores improves (or otherwise affects) downstream fine-tuning performance. Without such a downstream-utility experiment, the connection between the score and actual training impact remains indirect.

Mislabeled-data detection is evaluated on only one binary VLM task with artificially flipped labels; there is no LLM mislabeling experiment, no evaluation on naturally noisy data, and no analysis of robustness to near-duplicate or overlapping train/validation inputs, which is exactly where the distinct-input assumption (Assumption 2) breaks down.

Comparison fairness and baseline scope raise questions: baselines are evaluated at their best checkpoint over training (a favorable selection criterion), and only efficiency-oriented baselines are included; no comparison to stronger but costlier reference points (e.g., exact influence on LoRA subspaces, or DataShapley on a small subset) to anchor the accuracy claims.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and several details needed for exact reproduction (e.g., how the restricted vocabulary is defined per batch, hyperparameters of the score computation) are spread thinly across the text; reproducibility is currently uncertain.

Presentation issues: the α term sums over all cross token pairs (k, k') which can dilute the signal and is not analyzed; Figure 3 layout is confusing; minor typographical errors (e.g., 'Influencial'); Table 3's complexity notation uses inconsistent and partially undefined symbols (D, |V-hat|).

The framing that prior methods require 'fine-tuned weights inaccessible in practical deployments' overstates the limitation—gradient access during fine-tuning is commonly available to practitioners who would use data valuation in the first place, weakening the necessity argument for a forward-only method.

strengths: The central claim is well-motivated and clearly articulated: gradient-based data valuation (TracIn, DataInf, HyperINF, in-run Shapley) is prohibitively expensive for billion-parameter LLMs/VLMs because it requires per-sample backpropagation, while For-Value needs only a single forward pass and supports large-batch parallelism.

The theoretical derivation (Theorem 1/2) is correct as far as it goes: the last-layer (unembedding) gradient of the log-likelihood factors into an error-vector inner product times a hidden-state inner product, yielding a closed-form forward-computable score under the unconstrained-feature and distinct-input assumptions. Assumptions are stated explicitly, discussed, and placed in the context of prior LLM analyses (Mixon et al., Razin et al., Zhao et al.).

The sparse-vocabulary reformulation (Eq. 2, restricting to the in-batch/sample-associated vocabulary) is a sensible and well-explained engineering contribution that makes the score practical; the complexity comparison (Tab. 6) and runtime analysis (Fig. 4, Tab. 3-5) substantiate large efficiency gains (e.g., seconds vs. hours; scaling to 72B where baselines are impractical).

Empirical coverage is broad: influential-data identification and mislabeled detection on both LLMs (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-2-13B) and VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision), plus downstream data-selection experiments on GSM8K, a noisy medical CoT dataset, and PMC-Reasoning, with multiple seeds (mean±std reported).

Ablations support the design: removing the prediction-error term α reduces the method to embedding similarity (Emb), and the consistent gap over Emb isolates the value of the error-weighting term; results across model sizes (Fig. 3) show no degradation up to 72B.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: code is released, and the appendix provides training settings, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, task templates, and hardware details; honest disclosures include baseline checkpoint selection and LLM-usage statements.
weaknesses: The headline identification results (Tab. 1, 2) are obtained on small synthetic setups (10 classes, ~90 train/10 test per class; 600-sample style datasets) where strong baselines are already near ceiling (AUC ≈ 0.98-1.0). At saturation, differences of a few points in AUC/Recall are weak evidence, and the benchmarks do not probe the harder regime where valuation methods typically diverge (long-tail, ambiguous, or highly noisy data).

Novelty of the core technical observation is modest: the factorization of the last-layer softmax gradient into (e_y − π)h^T is classic, and last-layer/first-order gradient influence approximations are well established (Hessian-free/TracIn at the last iteration, first-order in-run Shapley). The contribution is largely a repackaging into a forward-only, sparse-vocabulary score; the paper would benefit from a more explicit positioning of what is genuinely new beyond this known algebra.

The theoretical result is a modeling approximation rather than a guarantee: under 'unconstrained features' hidden states are treated as free parameters, which makes the derivation essentially exact for the unembedding layer only, and ignores contributions of all other layers' parameters (interactions between hidden-state updates during training). No experiment directly validates Eq. (1) against the true d/dt log-likelihood change it is meant to approximate; the evidence is purely indirect via ranking tasks.

The distinct-input assumption (Assumption 2) that zeroes out Term (II) is stronger than the paper suggests: template-generated tasks (sentence transformations, math word problems) and prefix-sharing in autoregressive generation make identical or near-identical (x, y_<k) prefixes plausible, exactly where the neglected unembedding term matters. The claimed 'straightforward extension' is not analyzed or tested.

Data-selection experiments use test reasoning examples as the valuation set (acknowledged for GSM8K: 'as expected when using test data for valuation'), introducing a selection-vs-test overlap concern; comparisons across methods remain fair, but absolute claims about practical data selection are weakened, and no held-out-valuation variant is reported.

Downstream gains are mixed in magnitude: For-Value is clearly best on GSM8K and Noise-Huatuo, but on PMC-Reasoning at 20% it trails HyperINF (52.67 vs 53.04) and gains at 10% are +0.6 average; given near-saturated identification metrics and no error bars on fine-tuning results, the downstream-utility evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive.

Mislabeled-data detection is evaluated on a single small binary dataset (cat-vs-dog, 400 images/class, one noise ratio in the main table); generalization of the mislabeling claim to realistic LLM noise types is not established.

Writing has notable rough edges: awkward theorem statements ('the training data exhibits larger value to the valuation data as the following increases'), typos ('volcabulary', 'Most Influencial'), and a run-on related-work paragraph; the caption of Tab. 2 and footnote 2 hint at metric-definition ambiguities (polarized value distributions, rounding) that deserve cleaner treatment.

strengths: The core idea—deriving a forward-only, closed-form surrogate for last-layer gradient influence, enabling batch-parallel valuation without backpropagation—is practically appealing and clearly motivated for billion-parameter LLMs/VLMs.

The paper provides a full derivation (Appendix B) of the main score under an explicit assumption set, along with a complexity comparison (Tab. 6) and an ablation isolating the prediction-error weighting term α against the embedding-similarity (Emb) baseline.

Experiments are broad in coverage: two LLMs and two VLMs for identification tasks, data-selection experiments on GSM8K, a noisy medical CoT dataset, and PMC-Reasoning, with runtime scaling studies up to 72B parameters—something gradient-based baselines cannot support.

Reproducibility support is reasonable: code is released, hyperparameters, hardware, dataset statistics (Tab. 11), and task templates are documented in the appendix, and there is a limitations section and an LLM-usage disclosure.
weaknesses: The evaluation is saturated and therefore weakly diagnostic. On the LLM influential-data tasks (Tab. 1), both For-Value and gradient baselines reach AUC ≈ 1.000 and Recall ≈ 1.0; with reported standard deviations, claimed gains (e.g., 6.5% recall over HyperINF) fall within or near noise. The synthetic task design (e.g., unique 'chatbot' names prepended per transformation class, ten highly templated classes) plausibly makes class membership trivially recoverable from surface features, so near-perfect scores across all methods do not strongly validate the method.

The theoretical derivation rests on very strong idealizations that are presented as 'mild'. The unconstrained-features assumption treats all hidden states h and the unembedding matrix W as free, independent trainable parameters, ignoring that real gradients propagate through shared network weights; the proof also discards Term (II) via Assumption 2 (no training input equals the valuation input). The claim that this assumption is mild is asserted rather than analyzed, and no experiment quantifies the approximation error of the closed-form score relative to the true last-layer gradient it purports to capture.

Potential evaluation contamination in the headline data-selection result: GSM8K selection uses test reasoning examples as valuation data (acknowledged in Sec. 5.2), and For-Value is the only method not requiring a LoRA warm-up on the full training set in some settings, complicating attribution of its gains.

Claims of superiority are overstated relative to the evidence. On PMC-Reasoning at 20% data, HyperINF achieves a higher average (53.04 vs. 52.67) and several per-dataset wins, yet the text frames For-Value as delivering 'the strongest overall performance'; similarly, several VLM identification results show For-Value behind baselines on individual metrics.

Fair-comparison concerns in the efficiency analysis: baselines are evaluated on only one task, with 10% of valuation data subsampled and runtimes extrapolated by a factor of 10 for 14B/32B models, and quantization applied to baselines but not For-Value. The reported speedups may not reflect like-for-like conditions.
Baselines receive favorable checkpoint selection (best test AUC checkpoint per A.6.1), which is defensible for robustness but is selected using test-derived metrics, again blurring the evaluation.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: title capitalization ('finetuning'), repeated and inconsistent citations (two separate Qwen2.5-VL entries with the same arXiv ID; Yang et al. 2023 cited for GPT-4V), typos ('Influencial', 'volume' in Algorithm 1, 'volcabulary'), and loose wording ('as expected when using test data for valuation') that undercuts rigor.

The ablation study is thin: the α ablation is essentially re-labelled as the Emb baseline, model-size analysis (Fig. 3) reports near-constant AUC ≈ 1.0 (again saturated), and there is no analysis of failure modes, sensitivity to valuation-set choice, or behavior when hidden-representation alignment is a poor proxy (e.g., tasks requiring genuinely new knowledge rather than pattern matching).
